name: Cloudflare ChaCha20-Poly1305 OpenSSL patch (sslconfig)
workload: ChaCha20-Poly1305 AEAD 'seal' operation with 13 bytes of AAD (TLS-record-shaped), plaintext sizes from 64 bytes to 16 KB, on a Haswell-generation CPU
claimed_speedup: Cloudflare's patched ChaCha20-Poly1305 significantly outperforms OpenSSL 1.1.0-pre for short records and is slightly faster for long records, average advantage ~7%; the post also notes AES-128/256-GCM (with AES-NI) still beat ChaCha20-Poly1305 for records over 320 bytes, reaching below 2 cycles/byte
hardware: Haswell-generation CPU (exact model not stated); post notes Broadwell/Skylake give AES-GCM a further edge
tradeoffs: Patch targets OpenSSL's cipher-suite ordering/implementation for TLS ChaCha20-Poly1305, supporting both the pre-RFC draft and RFC 7905 cipher-suite IDs
caveats: Numbers are read off graphs in the post, not a data table; no compiler flags stated; the post dates to April 2016 and benchmarks an OpenSSL 1.1.0 pre-release, so absolute figures are stale even though the qualitative result (near-parity/slight win over stock OpenSSL ChaCha20-Poly1305 for short records) is historically well known. repo_url is on the KNOWN_LIST (already catalogued), reported here only as evidence for that known entry per is_evidence_for_known.
found_via: WebFetch of https://blog.cloudflare.com/it-takes-two-to-chacha-poly/, reached via HN Algolia search 'AES-NI vs ChaCha20' comment thread

name: AEGIS (AEGIS-128x2 / AEGIS-128x4)
workload: AEAD encryption/decryption throughput at 64 KB messages on Apple M5 Max, vs OpenSSL's AES-128-GCM backend
claimed_speedup: AEGIS-128x2 AEAD encryption 211.8 Gbps vs OpenSSL AES-128-GCM 70.8 Gbps at 64KB on M5 Max (~3x, derived from page data)
tradeoffs: Requires AES-NI/VAES/AVX-512 (x86) or ARM crypto extensions for peak throughput; unlike HiAE/ROCCA-S, AEGIS decrypts as fast as it encrypts (no AES-round latency in its keystream path)
caveats: AEGIS is already catalogued (KNOWN_LIST: github.com/aegis-aead/libaegis and github.com/aegis-aead/aegis-bitsliced). Included only as new tier-A evidence from hiae-aead/benchmarks, a reproducible harness with stated compiler/flags/CPU/OpenSSL version. Independently corroborated by mumble-voip/crypto-benchmark (tier B, GitHub Actions, 2024 snapshot): libsodium's AEGIS-128L at 0.647s vs OpenSSL AES-256-GCM at 2.525s for 1M x 4096-byte iterations (~3.9x), and vs OpenSSL ChaCha20-Poly1305 at 4.273s (~6.6x).
found_via: GitHub: search 'AEAD in:readme benchmark AES-NI' -> hiae-aead/benchmarks

name: HiAE
workload: AEAD encryption/decryption throughput at 64 KB messages on Apple M5 Max and AMD Zen 4, vs OpenSSL's AES-128-GCM backend
claimed_speedup: HiAE AEAD encryption 266.7 Gbps vs OpenSSL AES-128-GCM 70.8 Gbps at 64KB on M5 Max (~3.8x, derived from page data); 268.4 Gbps on Zen 4
hardware: Apple Silicon M5 Max (macOS 26); AMD Ryzen 7 7700 (Zen 4) at fixed 3.8GHz
tradeoffs: Decryption is up to 1.9x slower than encryption at 64KB (Zen4: 139.1 vs 268.4 Gbps) because the AES-round-then-fold state update recovers the message block only after the AES round finishes; multi-lane HiAEx2/HiAEx4 narrow this gap but need AVX-512+VAES on x86 or fall back to a much slower portable path
caveats: HiAE is already catalogued (KNOWN_LIST: github.com/concyclics/hiae). Included only as new tier-A evidence from hiae-aead/benchmarks. GitHub's license API returns 404 for concyclics/hiae (no detected LICENSE file), so usability is recorded as 'reference' for this specific repo even though a newer, MIT-licensed copy of the same algorithm exists at github.com/hiae-aead/libhiae (not filed as a separate entry since it is the same project/algorithm, just a different org).
found_via: GitHub: search 'AEAD in:readme benchmark AES-NI' -> hiae-aead/benchmarks

name: HiAE
workload: AEAD encryption/decryption throughput at 64KB messages, 4096-byte-aligned buffers, key/nonce setup included
claimed_speedup: HiAE AEAD encryption 266.7 Gbps vs AES-128-GCM 70.8 Gbps (~3.8x) at 64KB on Apple Silicon M5 Max (Apple clang 21.0.0, OpenSSL 3.6.4); 268.4 Gbps AEAD encryption on AMD Ryzen 7 7700 'Zen 4' (clang 21.1.8, -O3 -march=native, OpenSSL 3.5.5)
hardware: Apple Silicon M5 Max, macOS 26; AMD Ryzen 7 7700 'Zen 4' fixed at 3.8GHz, performance governor, turbo/frequency-scaling disabled
tradeoffs: Decryption up to ~1.93x slower than encryption on Zen4 (message block only recoverable after an AES round, same asymmetry class as Rocca-S); multi-lane HiAEx2/HiAEx4 variants trade some single-stream throughput for AVX-512/VAES parallelism
caveats: This is a Tier A independent benchmark (compiler, flags and CPU model all stated, code public) for a project already on the excluded/known list (concyclics/hiae); reported here as supplementary evidence per the is_evidence_for_known exception rather than as a new catalog entry. GitHub detects no license file for concyclics/hiae, so usability is recorded as reference pending confirmation
found_via: SUPERCOP eBACS AEAD benchmark fastest implementations -> gh search repos 'AEAD benchmark' -> hiae-aead/benchmarks (angt/hiae-bench-results mirror of the same suite)

name: ChainHash
workload: Bulk hashing of 256 KiB messages, measured in bytes/cycle, using the SMHasher3 protocol on the same compiled binaries for every hash; short-input case also measured (1-31 byte messages, cycles/hash).
claimed_speedup: Bulk: 28.31 B/cycle (Xeon 8375C) and 26.26 B/cycle (Apple M2 Pro) for ChainHash-64 vs 19.69 B/cycle (Xeon) and 13.16 B/cycle (M2) for XXH3-64 in the same binaries -- author states ChainHash 'had the highest throughput among all the hashes on Intel Xeon, second highest on Apple M2 Pro' (derived ratio from page data: ~1.4x Xeon, ~2.0x M2). ChainHash-128 is slower than XXH3-128 in the same test (14.43 vs 19.82 B/cycle Xeon; 10.26 vs 12.53 B/cycle M2). Short inputs (1-31 bytes) are much slower than XXH3-64: 155.14 vs 30.16 cycles/hash (Xeon), 87.49 vs 24.51 cycles/hash (M2).
tradeoffs: Only competitive with xxHash for long/bulk inputs; per-call setup and three serial finalizer multiplications make it far slower than XXH3 for short (<32 byte) keys. In exchange it carries a machine-checked (Lean-proved) >=63-bit universal collision bound, whereas XXH3 is only a heuristic construction with no such proof (the same blog post documents seed-independent collision weaknesses in XXH3 and many other popular hashes).
caveats: thomasahle/chainhash is already in the known-list (KNOWN_LIST), so this entry is submitted only as new Tier-A evidence for a known project (is_evidence_for_known=true), per the exception in the assignment rules, not as a new candidate to add. Benchmark is first-party (by ChainHash's own author) but unusually rigorous: exact CPU models stated, 'same binaries' controlled comparison across all hashes, SMHasher3 commit pinned (7ad8939d), and a public reproduction package is linked; independent third-party confirmation was not found. Exact compiler and optimization flags for the throughput table specifically were not located in the fetched text (an interactive chart), hence compiler_and_flags=null despite otherwise strong methodology.
